result:
`is_supported_version` in `mitmproxy/net/tls.py` now returns `False` when setting the min or max protocol version raises `SSL.Error`, instead of letting the error escape. Some OpenSSL builds reject versions they were compiled without, and this treats those versions as unsupported. I haven't run the tests, as you asked.

I added `test_supported_set_version_error` to `test/mitmproxy/net/test_tls.py`. It patches `SSL.Context.set_min_proto_version` to raise `SSL.Error` and checks the function returns `False`. The test calls `is_supported_version.__wrapped__` because the function is `@cache`d and a cached result would hide the patch.

--- a/mitmproxy/net/tls.py
+++ b/mitmproxy/net/tls.py
@@ -77,8 +77,12 @@ def is_supported_version(version: Version):
     # Without SECLEVEL, recent OpenSSL versions forbid old TLS versions.
     # https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/issues/9523
     client_ctx.set_cipher_list(b"@SECLEVEL=0:ALL")
-    client_ctx.set_min_proto_version(version.value)
-    client_ctx.set_max_proto_version(version.value)
+    try:
+        client_ctx.set_min_proto_version(version.value)
+        client_ctx.set_max_proto_version(version.value)
+    except SSL.Error:
+        # Some OpenSSL builds reject versions they were compiled without.
+        return False
     client_conn = SSL.Connection(client_ctx)
     client_conn.set_connect_state()
